quests.instruction: In the middle of each eye is a small black circle that lets light in. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is a round opening, like a tiny window.
quests.explanation: The pupil is an opening in the middle of the eye. Light passes through it so you can see.
quests.funFact: Your pupils get smaller in bright light and bigger in dim light.

quests.instruction: A butterfly flutters from flower to flower. Which body parts follow it as it moves?
quests.hint: Your head can stay still while these swivel from side to side.
quests.explanation: Your eyes can turn up, down, and sideways to follow moving things, even when your head stays still.
quests.funFact: When you read, your eyes do not glide smoothly. They hop from word to word in tiny jumps.

quests.instruction: You step into a room with no windows and no lights. Which one of these stops being useful?
quests.hint: It needs light to work.
quests.explanation: You see when light bounces off things and into your eyes. With no light at all, your eyes have nothing to catch.
quests.funFact: A cat's eyes have a mirror-like layer that helps them use dim light, which is why they seem to glow in headlights.

quests.instruction: At a check-up, a doctor asks you to read letters off a chart on the wall. Which body parts is the doctor testing?
quests.hint: You use them for reading and watching cartoons.
quests.explanation: Reading smaller and smaller letters shows how clearly your eyes see far away. If letters look blurry, glasses can help.
quests.funFact: Children's eyes are still developing in the early years, so regular eye check-ups matter.

quests.instruction: Your eyes send signals toward the middle of your head. Which part turns those signals into the pictures you see?
quests.hint: It is protected inside your skull.
quests.explanation: Your brain puts together the signals from your eyes, so you can notice faces, colors, and movement.
quests.funFact: Each eye sees a slightly different view, and your brain blends the two into one picture.

quests.instruction: You stand on the sidewalk, well away from the road, with your eyes shut. Which body parts can still tell you a car is coming?
quests.hint: They catch sounds from all around you.
quests.explanation: Sounds travel through the air, so you can hear a car without looking at it. That is why listening matters near roads.
quests.funFact: Quiet electric cars are harder to hear, so looking both ways matters, too.

quests.instruction: Deep inside your ear is a thin, stretchy skin that wobbles when sound reaches it, a bit like the top of a drum. What is it called?
quests.hint: Sound makes it vibrate.
quests.explanation: When sound waves reach the eardrum, it vibrates. The vibrations are passed along until nerves send a message to your brain.
quests.funFact: Your eardrum is thinner than a sheet of paper.

quests.instruction: A jackhammer is breaking up the sidewalk, and it is very loud. Which body parts need protection from the noise?
quests.hint: Workers wear special muffs over them.
quests.explanation: Very loud noise can damage the delicate parts inside your ear, so people near loud machines wear ear protection.
quests.funFact: Hearing damage from loud noise can be permanent.

quests.instruction: Which soft, squishy part hangs down at the bottom of your ear?
quests.hint: People sometimes wear earrings on it.
quests.explanation: The earlobe is the soft bottom edge of your outer ear.
quests.funFact: Earlobes have no bone or stiff cartilage inside, which is why they are so soft.

quests.instruction: A bird chirps on your left side. Which body parts help you work out which side the sound came from?
quests.hint: You have one on each side of your head.
quests.explanation: Sound reaches the closer ear a tiny bit sooner and a little louder, and your brain uses that to tell where the sound came from.
quests.funFact: Some owls have ears at slightly different heights, which helps them find prey in the dark.

quests.instruction: Put your fingers lightly on the front of your neck and hum. You feel a buzzing. Which part is making the sound?
quests.hint: It is inside your neck, and air passes through it.
quests.explanation: Your voice starts in your throat, where two folds called vocal cords vibrate as air passes over them.
quests.funFact: Your vocal cords vibrate hundreds of times every second when you speak.

quests.instruction: Sticky mucus inside which part catches dust before it travels toward your lungs?
quests.hint: Blowing it into a tissue clears out the sticky stuff.
quests.explanation: Mucus inside your nose is sticky, so dust and germs get stuck in it instead of traveling farther into your body.
quests.funFact: A sneeze is a fast blast of air that blows trapped dust out of your nose.

quests.instruction: A smoky smell drifts out of the kitchen. Which body part notices it?
quests.hint: It sniffs the air.
quests.explanation: Your nose can smell smoke before you see any flames. If you smell smoke, tell a grown-up right away.
quests.funFact: Smell does not reliably wake people up, which is why smoke alarms are so important.

quests.instruction: A dog follows a trail across the grass with its head low. Which part of the dog is doing the main work?
quests.hint: It is wet, black, and sniffing hard.
quests.explanation: Dogs follow trails mostly by smell, and a dog's nose can pick out many scents at once.
quests.funFact: A dog's sense of smell is many times stronger than yours.

quests.instruction: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter: which part of your mouth can tell these tastes apart?
quests.hint: It also moves food around while you chew.
quests.explanation: Taste buds on your tongue sense sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and a savory taste, and send messages about them to your brain.
quests.funFact: Taste buds are replaced every couple of weeks.

quests.instruction: You pinch your nose shut while eating a jelly bean, and the flavor almost disappears. Which part, besides your tongue, helps you notice flavor?
quests.hint: It brings smells from your food up to your brain.
quests.explanation: Much of what you call flavor is really smell. When your nose is blocked, food tastes plain.
quests.funFact: Flavor is a mix of taste, smell, texture, and even temperature.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body should never be used to test an unknown berry?
quests.hint: It is where food goes in.
quests.explanation: Some wild berries and plants are poisonous, even if they look like fruit. Always ask a grown-up before putting anything unknown into your mouth.
quests.funFact: Birds can eat some berries that are poisonous to people.

quests.instruction: You wrap yourself in a soft, fuzzy blanket. Which part of your body covers all of you and feels the softness?
quests.hint: It covers your whole body from head to toe.
quests.explanation: Skin is full of tiny touch sensors that notice soft, rough, smooth, and bumpy things.
quests.funFact: Skin is the largest organ in your body.

quests.instruction: You touch a hot cup and snatch your hand away before you even think about it. Which part felt the heat and sent the alarm?
quests.hint: It covers your fingers and feels hot and cold.
quests.explanation: Touch sensors in your skin notice heat and send a fast message, so your hand pulls away before you have time to think.
quests.funFact: The message to pull away takes a shortcut through your spinal cord, which makes it faster than thinking.

quests.instruction: People who are blind can read raised dots called braille. Which parts of the body do they use to feel the dots?
quests.hint: They are very sensitive to small bumps.
quests.explanation: Fingertips are packed with touch sensors, so they can feel tiny differences in texture.
quests.funFact: Braille was invented by Louis Braille, who was fifteen when he developed the system.

quests.instruction: You climb out of a pool on a chilly day, and little bumps pop up on your arms. Which part of your body shows goosebumps?
quests.hint: It covers the whole outside of you.
quests.explanation: Tiny muscles in your skin pull the hairs upright when you are cold or startled, and that makes the bumps.
quests.funFact: Long ago, our ancestors had thicker body hair, and standing hairs helped trap warm air.

quests.instruction: Which hard, flat parts at the tips of your fingers protect them and help you pick up tiny things like a coin?
quests.hint: You trim them when they get too long.
quests.explanation: Fingernails shield your fingertips and give them something firm to press against, which helps you grip and feel small things.
quests.funFact: Fingernails grow faster than toenails.

quests.instruction: Which thin, thread-like pathways carry messages between your skin and your brain?
quests.hint: They work like wires, sending messages quickly.
quests.explanation: Nerves carry signals from your senses to your brain, and they send instructions back to your muscles.
quests.funFact: Fast nerve messages can travel over 100 meters every second.

quests.instruction: A tiny seed gets stuck between your teeth. Which part of your mouth can feel it right away?
quests.hint: It is a soft, very bendy muscle.
quests.explanation: Your tongue is very sensitive to touch, so it can find even a tiny seed or a single hair.
quests.funFact: Besides tasting, your tongue is one of the most touch-sensitive parts of your body.

quests.instruction: When an airplane climbs or lands, which part of your body might feel a popping pressure?
quests.hint: Yawning or swallowing can help.
quests.explanation: Air pressure changes outside, and your ears adjust. Swallowing or yawning opens a tiny tube so the pressure evens out.
quests.funFact: That tube connects the inside of your ear to the back of your throat.

quests.instruction: A person who is deaf watches a friend's hands to understand sign language. Which body parts do they use to see the signs?
quests.hint: They notice shapes and movement.
quests.explanation: Sign language is made with the hands, face, and body, and you see it with your eyes.
quests.funFact: Sign languages have their own grammar, and they are not the same in every country.

quests.instruction: Eardrums, earlobes, and pupils are all parts of the head, but one of them belongs to a different sense organ. Which one?
quests.hint: One of them belongs to the eye.
quests.explanation: Eardrums and earlobes belong to the ear. Pupils are the black circles in the middle of the eyes.
quests.funFact: The three tiny bones in your middle ear are the smallest bones in your body.

quests.instruction: Which part of your mouth helps you taste and also helps you talk?
quests.hint: It does two jobs in your mouth.
quests.explanation: The tongue senses tastes, and it also moves to shape sounds into words.
quests.funFact: Taste buds are not only on the tongue. Some are on the roof of your mouth and in your throat.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body lets you feel touch and also keeps water and germs out?
quests.hint: It covers your whole body.
quests.explanation: Skin has touch sensors, and it also works like a waterproof wrapper that keeps most germs out.
quests.funFact: The outer layer of your skin is replaced about every month.

quests.instruction: A bite of very cold ice cream sends a sharp twinge through which hard parts of your mouth?
quests.hint: They have nerves inside, even though the outside is hard.
quests.explanation: Inside each tooth are nerves, so teeth can feel cold, heat, and pain, especially if the hard outer layer is worn or damaged.
quests.funFact: Dentists sometimes use dental records to help identify people.
